title: Merge Transcript Segments
statement:
A speech engine streams a meeting transcript as short segments. Each segment is [speaker, start_ms, end_ms, text]. Segments can arrive out of order (the engine finishes some audio chunks before others), and one person talking for a minute shows up as many small pieces. Before you show the transcript, or send it to a model to pull out decisions, you want one row per speaking turn.

Write def solution(segments) that returns the merged turns as a list of [speaker, start_ms, end_ms, text]:

  1. Sort the segments by start_ms. Segments with the same start_ms keep their input order.
  2. Walk them in that order. A segment joins the previous turn when it has the same speaker and its gap is at most 1500 ms: start_ms - turn_end ≤ 1500. An overlap (negative gap) also joins.
  3. When a segment joins, the turn keeps its start, its end becomes max(turn_end, end_ms), and the text becomes turn_text + " " + text.
  4. Otherwise the segment starts a new turn. A different speaker always starts a new turn, even if the earlier speaker talks again right after.

Return the turns in time order. An empty input returns [].

examples.why: Sort by start: A@0, A@1100, B@1400. The two A pieces are 100 ms apart, so they join. B is a different speaker, so it starts a new turn.
The gap 2500 - 1000 = 1500 is allowed, so "second" joins. The next gap is 4501 - 3000 = 1501, one over the limit, so "third" starts a new turn.
"um" overlaps the first turn and ends earlier, so the turn keeps end 5000. B speaks next, which closes A's turn; A talking again at 3200 is a third turn.

constraints: speaker is a non-empty string; text is a non-empty string with no leading or trailing spaces
segments may overlap in time, including segments from different speakers

think.q: What is the output, in one sentence?
think.a: The same segments, sorted by start, with runs of one speaker glued together whenever the pause between pieces is 1500 ms or less.
Sort: 0, 1200, 2000. 1200 - 900 = 300: join, end 1800, text "hi there". 2000 - 1800 = 200: join, end 2500. Result [[A, 0, 2500, "hi there all"]].
For each segment, search all the others for the next one by the same speaker. That is O(n^2) and it gets the "a different speaker breaks the run" rule wrong, because it skips over other speakers.
"out of order", "consecutive", "gap" → sort, then one linear merge pass. It is the same shape as merging overlapping intervals: after sorting, each item only needs to look at the last output row.

1. sorted(segments, key=start).
  2. For each segment: if the last turn has the same speaker and start - last_end ≤ 1500, extend it.
  3. Else append a copy of the segment as a new turn.
  4. Return the turns.

Empty input. A gap of exactly 1500 (joins) and 1501 (splits). An overlapping segment that ends before the turn ends (the end must not shrink). Same start time twice. A, B, A with short gaps (three turns, not two). Mutating the caller's lists by accident.

hints: Sort first: sorted(segments, key=lambda seg: seg[1]). Python's sort is stable, which gives you the tie rule for free.
After sorting you only ever compare a segment with the last turn you produced, never with older ones.
When you extend a turn use max(last_end, end): an overlapping short segment can end before the turn does. Append [speaker, start, end, text] as a new list so you never edit the input.
solution:
MAX_GAP_MS = 1500   # a pause longer than this starts a new turn

def solution(segments):
    # 1. Put the segments in time order. sorted() is stable, so two segments
    #    with the same start keep the order the engine sent them in.
    ordered = sorted(segments, key=lambda seg: seg[1])

    turns = []
    for speaker, start, end, text in ordered:
        if turns:
            last = turns[-1]
            # 2. Same speaker as the previous turn, and the pause is short
            #    (an overlap gives a negative gap, which also counts as short)
            if last[0] == speaker and start - last[2] <= MAX_GAP_MS:
                last[2] = max(last[2], end)      # never move the end backwards
                last[3] = last[3] + ' ' + text
                continue
        # 3. Otherwise this segment opens a new turn (copy it: never mutate input)
        turns.append([speaker, start, end, text])
    return turns
explain:
Sorting turns a messy stream into a problem you can solve in one pass. Once segments are in start order, a segment can only join the turn right before it, so you keep a list of turns and look at turns[-1].

  • Input [B, 1400, 2000, "yes"], [A, 0, 1000, "can we"], [A, 1100, 1300, "ship it"].
  • Sorted: A@0, A@1100, B@1400.
  • A@1100: same speaker, gap 100 → turn A becomes [A, 0, 1300, "can we ship it"].
  • B@1400: different speaker → new turn.

In a live round, name the two rules that are easy to get wrong before you code: the end must use max, and another speaker in between always splits. Then write those as tests.
complexity: O(n log n) time for the sort, O(n) for the output

tests.label: example 1
tests.why: out of order; same speaker joins, new speaker splits

tests.label: example 3 (overlap and interleave)
tests.why: end uses max; another speaker in between always splits

tests.label: one segment
tests.why: a single segment is one turn

tests.label: same start time
tests.why: ties keep input order: x before y

tests.label: chain at the limit
tests.why: each gap is exactly 1500 until the last (1501)

tests.label: zero-length segments
tests.why: start == end, gap 0, identical text is still joined

tests.label: backchannel
tests.why: B says "mm" during A; sorted order is A, B, A so there are three turns

tests.label: three speakers shuffled
tests.why: sorting plus merging across a shuffled meeting
